body:
The interfaces limit which methods are available through a value of that interface type.  While a value of type `FlaggableStore` doesn't have these methods, an `ImageStore` value, which is of a type that embeds both `ROImageStore` and `FlaggableStore`, includes both (and more), and that's what we actually use.
They're sliced up like this to avoid having any given method appear more than once in an interface, whether directly or through embedding.  The compiler rejected that kind of duplication as an error when I first tried it.
The method implementations receive the underlying object type, so they're free to call any method that the object implements.
If we implemented read-only and read-write stores as different object types in addition to different interface types, we wouldn't need to check for read-only status in several of the write methods.  We're adding those checks just to be safe in case someone decides to try using a type assertion to convert a read-only interface type to a read-write interface.  The object that underlies a read-only interface value also provides all of the methods of the read-write interface, so it wouldn't cause an error.

+We'd love to have you join the community! Below summarizes the processes

+
+## Topics

+* [Reporting Issues](#reporting-issues)

+## Reporting Issues
+
+Before reporting an issue, check our backlog of 
+[open issues](https://github.com/containers/storage/issues)
+to see if someone else has already reported it. If so, feel free to add
+your scenario, or additional information, to the discussion. Or simply 
+"subscribe" to it to be notified when it is updated.
+
+If you find a new issue with the project we'd love to hear about it! The most
+important aspect of a bug report is that it includes enough information for
+us to reproduce it. So, please include as much detail as possible and try
+to remove the extra stuff that doesn't really relate to the issue itself.
+The easier it is for us to reproduce it, the faster it'll be fixed!
+
+Please don't include any private/sensitive information in your issue!
+

+
+No Pull Request (PR) is too small! Typos, additional comments in the code,
+new testcases, bug fixes, new features, more documentation, ... it's all 
+welcome!
+
+While bug fixes can first be identified via an "issue", that is not required.
+It's ok to just open up a PR with the fix, but make sure you include the same
+information you would have included in an issue - like how to reproduce it.
+
+PRs for new features should include some background on what use cases the
+new code is trying to address. When possible and when it makes sense, try to break-up
+larger PRs into smaller ones - it's easier to review smaller
+code changes. But only if those smaller ones make sense as stand-alone PRs.
+
+Regardless of the type of PR, all PRs should include:
+* well documented code changes
+* additional testcases. Ideally, they should fail w/o your code change applied
+* documentation changes

+separate from the rest of the PRs. But, squashing down to just one commit is ok
+too since in the end the entire PR will be reviewed anyway. When in doubt,

+commit message so that github will automatically close the referenced issue
+when the PR is merged.

body:
Throughout this function, in both implementations:

- Use `path` instead of `os.Args[1]`
- `return fmt.Errorf(…)` instead of `Fprintf`+`Exit`.

Both of these are already done in the caller, and logically belong at the top level.  (Well, except that the caller uses `os.Args[`**`0`**`]`, so one of them must be incorrect.)

> We've seen permissions-related problems preventing us from launching containers using user namespaces when they were using root directories which had some parent directory wasn't at least searchable by the UID/GID that we were mapping to 0/0 for the container.

(General comment, applies to most of the `0711` changes, and I am probably missing a long previous conversation:)

It’s not obvious to me why this should be the case.  Isn’t the container started by the host-level `root`? In that case, it naively seems to me that host-level `root` should be able to `chroot` into the root directory of the container, or set up a new namespace, however strict the permissions are, drop privileges, and then `chdir .` (or `chdir /`) without needing to touch any of the parents of that path, and therefore I would expect that the permissions of the parents don’t matter.  Only the root of the namespace, and maybe directories created inside that root of the namespace, should need to be searchable by the processes restricted by the container / user namespaces AFAICT. Having the parents inaccessible could actually work as another layer of protection against a `chroot`/namespace breakout, which seems desirable.

Why make this change?

`&s` always point to the same memory as the loop variable is allocated only once, even for non-primitive types. What happens when using `defer s.Unlock()` in the loop is that we unlock the very same lock (always the last item in the slice) for `len(append([]ROImageStore{istore}, istores...))` times.

Ultimately, I want to remove all `defer lock.Unlock()` occurances in the code as it delays releasing the lock. The "trick" used in this commit is to allocate a new pointer on the heap `store := s` and use that in the defer statement.

Note that the issue of using loop variables in go applies to other cases as well. I wrote a blog about that last April (https://vrothberg.github.io/2018/04/02/pointers-in-golang-considered-harmful.html).

Note that this particular problem of unlocking the same lock multiple times predates this PR. I am a bit surprised that it did not cause (major) issues yet as it implies that some lock remained unlocked and others have been unlocked too often.
Nice catch, thanks! Just updated the PR.

body: Using a mutex here is very smart! I first felt that's not necessary but we're serializing the goroutines here and rely on the correctness of the mutex instead of relying on the correctness of the lock we're testing. Really nice!

Hmm, at this point I don't think so.  I know at one point we wanted to refactor interfaces so that Store wasn't just one large interface of its own, but that hasn't really bought us much since then.

The logic for quietly backfilling in a value when there isn't one recorded is there for upgrade cases where the previously-used version didn't track item digests, but that was something we added in #109, so it could also be argued that we don't need to worry about those cases any more.

Dropping both of those would let us excise the need for the callback everywhere except for in `SetImageBigData()`, which might be worth it.

This is now being addressed in the latest commit:
```
Add a method to the store to generate a lock file for a specific digest.
Such a digest-specific lock file is needed to synchronize threads and
processes when copying blobs from a registry to the containers-storage.

Whenever a layer is about to get copied, the lock must be acquired which
indicates to other processes and threads that the layer/blob is already
being copied.

To avoid leaking file descriptors, add a new Close() method to the
Locker.  We are now counting references on locks, which are being
decremented in Close().  When the last reference called Close(),
the lock file's FD is being closed as well.  The reference counter is
incremented for each new invocation on Get{RO,}Lockfile().
```

In short: we're now reference counting the lock files and have a `Locker.Close()` method which will close the file descriptor when the reference counter is 0.

The store now just returns a locker, while the storage image destination must take care of book keeping of the Locker objects.

I think this means the Ubuntu runs will take twice as long, and there will be two integration-test outputs one after another.  This became a headache in libpod, where we had the remote integration tests following the regular ones.

Brent and I fixed this, using a Cirrus-CI mechanism that makes it [simple to automatically duplicate a task with a slight modification, like a different env. var. value.](https://github.com/containers/libpod/blob/master/.cirrus.yml#L272-L275)  
  Then at [runtime, both run in paralle but behave differently depending on the env. var value.](https://github.com/containers/libpod/blob/master/contrib/cirrus/integration_test.sh#L41-L45)  Therefor they have separate outputs, and all else is equal.

body:
It could be that I'm reading the script wrong, but I see ``make STORAGE_DRIVER=overlay ... local-test-integration`` always, then for Ubuntu it also does 'make STORAGE_DRIVER=aufs local-test-integration'.  So I'm assuming `local-test-integration` == `local-test-integration` (time-wise) which could be wrong.

So what can happen is, somebody is debugging an Ubuntu problem, and looks at the output in the cirrus WebUI.  They see integration test output, and assume it's the `STORAGE_DRIVER=overlay` variety.  In reality, Cirrus-CI has truncated the output, and is showing the Ubuntu case with `STORAGE_DRIVER=aufs`.  This can cost the poor debugger lots of wasted time.  It isn't a problem if the tests all clearly identify the storage-driver they use, but poking through results here I didn't see that.
